687.title: What you keep
687.hook: three Stoic habits that fit your life
687.howItsDone: Some people finishing a period of Stoic study choose a small number of practices, often three, that they will keep using daily, and write them down.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Chrysippus, who thought only the souls of the wise last until the world's burning. Your line was what it leaves open.

Open almost any kitchen drawer and you'll find the gadgets: a garlic press, an egg slicer, a cherry pitter used once. Then there's what actually gets reached for every night: one good knife, one pan, a wooden spoon. Nobody plans that short list. Use writes it. This year on the path has handed you a lot: morning previews, evening questions, two handles, two cities, the view from above, the ripe olive. Most of it can stay in the drawer.
screen: `A DRAWER FULL OF GADGETS.` → `ONE KNIFE, ONE PAN, ONE SPOON.` → `A YEAR OF PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: First, Seneca on books. In one of his earliest letters to Lucilius, he warns against reading too many authors, skipping from one to the next. Food thrown up as soon as it's swallowed doesn't nourish, he says, and a plant moved too often never grows. Better to stay with a few great minds and digest them, and each day choose one thought to carry. That's this week's spirit: not everything, but a few things, really digested. Second, Epictetus on training. The Stoic word is askēsis: practice, training, the way an athlete trains. Every habit, Epictetus says, is built up and strengthened by the matching actions: walking by walking, running by running. Want to be good at something? Do it. Don't want a habit? Stop feeding it. So the habits you keep are the ones you'll actually do, not the ones you admire. Third, how to choose your three. Ask three questions of each practice from the year. Did I actually use it? Did it change a real day, even once? Does it fit the life I have, with my work, my family, my body, my beliefs? Someone might keep the evening review, the two columns, and delaying an angry reply. Someone else, the morning preview, the view from above, and love for the mortal. There's no right three. Fourth, why three. Few enough to remember without a list, and enough to cover morning, evening and the hard moments between. Epictetus told his students not to talk about their principles, but to show them by how they live. Three is a number you can show.

Your line: my three. A few habits, used, outweigh a drawer full of admired ones. That's day six hundred eighty-seven.

688.title: What you leave
688.hook: one Stoic idea that doesn't fit you
688.howItsDone: Some modern readers of the Stoics adopt some of their practices while openly setting aside others, such as the ideal of being free of all passions or the paradox that all wrongs are equal.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was askēsis, practice and training, habits built by doing. Your line was my three.

A friend lends you a cookbook from their grandmother's kitchen. You love it. You make the bread every Sunday now. But there's a chapter on organ meats that you read once, out of respect, and quietly decided was not for you. You didn't throw the book away. You didn't write an angry letter to the grandmother. You just left that chapter where it was. A year of Stoic reading can leave a chapter like that: an idea admired, or tried, or argued with, and finally set down.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER'S COOKBOOK.` → `BREAD EVERY SUNDAY.` → `ONE CHAPTER, LEFT WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: First, permission from Seneca himself. A committed Stoic, he still wrote that he hadn't bound himself to any one master or borne anyone's name. The great thinkers before us, he says in another letter, are not our masters but our guides. And he quoted Epicurus, a rival, again and again, taking what was good wherever he found it. Leaving something behind is, oddly, a very Senecan thing to do. Second, some candidates. Some readers find a few Stoic ideas hard to live with. The hope of being entirely free of passions, which can sound like numbness. The claim that health, wealth, even the people we love, are indifferent to our true good. The old Stoic paradox that all wrongdoing is equally wrong. Epictetus's hardest words about grief. None of these is a misreading; they really are in the texts. And serious Stoics, then and now, have argued about them too. Third, how to leave well. Not with contempt. Name the idea fairly, in its strongest form, the way the Stoics would state it. Then say plainly, without a fight: not for me. You may come back to it in ten years and find it fits. Or not. Fourth, why it matters. Seneca read his teachers as guides, keeping some things and leaving others, and the Stoic school itself kept arguing with its founders. Walking a philosophy as yourself is part of the tradition, not a break from it. The porch was always open on the sides. You can step off it, and step back on.

Notice that you can understand it and still not take it on. Then gently set it down, the way you'd close a chapter in a borrowed book: not for me, at least not now.

689.title: A year on the porch
689.hook: a year with Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus
689.howItsDone: Some people finishing a year of Stoic reading reread their earliest notes and ask how the practice has changed them, if at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epicurus, the rival Seneca quoted as a guide. Your line was not for me.

A merchant from Cyprus named Zeno has been shipwrecked and lost his cargo. Stranded in Athens, he wanders into a bookshop and hears someone reading about Socrates. He asks the bookseller: where can I find men like that? The story goes that a philosopher happened to walk past right then, and the bookseller pointed. Years later, Zeno began teaching in a public colonnade on the edge of the marketplace. That covered walkway gave the school its name, and gave this whole year its name too.
screen: `A SHIPWRECKED MERCHANT.` → `WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THAT?` → `A COLONNADE IN ATHENS.`

segments.voice: First, the porch itself. In Greek, stoa poikilē: the painted porch, a long roofed walkway whose walls carried famous paintings, including the battle of Marathon. Anyone could walk in. Zeno taught there, in public, and his followers were called the people of the stoa: Stoics. A philosophy named not after a founder but after a public place where anyone could stand and listen. Second, the road. It started on day three hundred thirty-two with a little handbook, Epictetus's teaching boiled down by his student Arrian, meant to be kept at hand. Then the longer Discourses, Epictetus arguing and joking with his students. Then Seneca, letter by letter, essay by essay. Then all twelve books of Marcus, straight through. And lately, the wider porch: the founders before, the neighbors next door, the people who came after, the turning year, and the porch in ordinary life. Third, four very different voices. A merchant who lost everything at sea. A man once enslaved, who limped. A rich adviser at a dangerous court. An emperor writing to himself on campaign. They didn't agree on everything, and they weren't saints. But each kept asking the same plain questions: what is up to me? What is good? How should I live with other people? Fourth, what a year does. One lesson is a thought. A year of them is a road, with your own days woven through it.

Maybe nothing obvious; that's honest too. Then let the year's voices pass by, Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus, and notice which one, if any, you'd most like to sit beside.

690.title: Thank the freed slave
690.hook: Epictetus, lame and once enslaved, taught an emperor through a book
690.howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus keep in mind that he was once enslaved and never wrote anything himself, and use that as a prompt to thank the unlikely people who have taught them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was stoa poikilē, the painted porch where Zeno taught. Your line was what is up to me.

Emperors had famous teachers: senators, celebrated scholars with big houses. This one's favorite reading came from somewhere else. A slave in Nero's Rome, walking with a limp. He never writes a book. He's eventually freed, teaches in Rome, is driven out of the city along with the other philosophers, and opens a school in a provincial town in Greece. And an emperor of Rome ends up reading his words, and thanks the friend who shared them. Three days of thanks begin here.
screen: `A SLAVE IN NERO'S ROME, WITH A LIMP.` → `FREED, EXILED, TEACHING IN GREECE.` → `AN EMPEROR READING HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, his name. Epiktētos is an ordinary Greek word meaning acquired, and some readers hear in it a slave's name: something bought. Nobody knows what his parents called him. Tradition says his owner was Epaphroditus, a freedman who served Nero. In the Discourses, Epictetus remembers his teacher Musonius Rufus testing him: what will you do when your master treats you badly? Second, his limp. Ancient writers didn't agree on how it happened. One story, preserved by Origen, says a master twisted his leg until it broke, while Epictetus calmly warned him it would. Another says it was illness. Nobody knows for sure. What is clear: the man who taught that lameness hinders the leg, not the will, was speaking from his own body. Third, the book he didn't write. Epictetus wrote nothing. His student Arrian took down his words as closely as he could, as reminders for himself, and in the letter at the front of the Discourses says the notes reached the public without his knowledge. Those notes, and the little Handbook, are nearly all we have of him. Fourth, the emperor. In the first book of the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius thanks his teacher Rusticus for many things, among them introducing him to Epictetus's teaching, sharing it from his own copy. So the chain goes: an enslaved man, a teacher, a student's notes, a friend's copy, an emperor's notebook, and, centuries later, you. The person at the start of that chain is the one nobody would have bet on.

691.title: Thank the courtier
691.hook: Seneca, flawed and rich, left the kindest letters
691.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca hold both his wisdom and his compromises in view at once, valuing the letters while seeing the man clearly.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epiktētos, Greek for acquired, the once-enslaved teacher. Your line was the unlikely teacher.

A coach who changed your life and also yelled too much. A professor whose ideas you still use, and who turned out to have behaved badly. A parent who taught kindness and wasn't always kind. Teachers like that are hard to put on a pedestal, and hard to throw away. Some readers put Seneca in exactly that spot. He wrote letters full of warmth and good sense. He was also enormously rich, and he spent years at the side of Nero.
screen: `A COACH WHO YELLED TOO MUCH.` → `NOT A PEDESTAL, NOT THE TRASH.` → `SENECA AT NERO'S SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the flaws, said plainly. Seneca was enormously wealthy, and ancient critics accused him of hypocrisy for preaching simplicity from his villas. He was Nero's tutor, then his adviser, and stayed on through dark years; the historian Tacitus reports that after Nero had his own mother killed, Seneca was believed to have written the letter Nero sent the Senate explaining it away. Earlier, exiled to Corsica, he wrote a consolation to a powerful official that reads, in places, like flattery aimed at winning his way home. Second, he knew. Seneca imagines his critics asking why he talks one way and lives another. He answers that he isn't wise, and isn't even close. He speaks about virtue, he says, not about himself, and when he criticizes faults, he includes his own. Third, the kindness. The letters to Lucilius are full of it: the people who serve us are human beings like us; tears for a friend are allowed; begin now; trust a true friend as you trust yourself. Fourth, the end. Accused of a part in a plot against Nero, Seneca was ordered to die. Tacitus tells us he asked for tablets to write his will and was refused. So he turned to his friends and said that since he couldn't repay them, he would leave them the one thing he still had, and the finest: the pattern of his life. Flawed and kind. Both true. You can thank him for the letters and still see the man clearly.

692.title: Thank the emperor
692.hook: Marcus wrote to no one and ended up writing to everyone
692.howItsDone: Many readers of the Meditations keep a private notebook of their own, writing short lines to themselves in the second person, the way Marcus did.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Tacitus, who told of Seneca's flaws and his last gift. Your line was flawed and kind.

A tent on the Danube frontier, sometime in the 170s, after dark. The man inside is the emperor of Rome, and he is writing in a private notebook, in Greek, to nobody. Not to the Senate. Not to his son. To himself. Get up, there's work to do. You'll meet difficult people today. You're getting angry again. Nobody was meant to read it. Today it sits on nightstands and in backpacks around the world. The last of three thank-yous.
screen: `A TENT ON THE FRONTIER, AFTER DARK.` → `WRITING TO NOBODY.` → `READ AROUND THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: First, a notebook with no reader. Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180, and spent much of his last decade at war in the north. Two of the books carry small notes of where they were written: among the Quadi, by the river Granua, and at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube. He never mentions publishing. He talks to himself as you, the way you talk to yourself in the car. Second, how close it came to vanishing. After his death the notebook goes almost silent in the record for centuries. Around the year 900, a Byzantine bishop named Arethas writes in a letter that he owns an old copy, worn and battered. The first printed edition came out in 1559, from a manuscript that is now lost. A private book, hanging by a thread. Third, why it reaches everyone. He wasn't performing. A speech has to look good; a note to yourself only has to be true. So Marcus admits things. Again and again he tells himself to stop getting angry. In book eight he orders himself: let no one hear you complaining about life at court any more, not even you. The ruler of an empire, caught grumbling, and catching himself. Fourth, how to thank him. Book one is itself a page of thanks: to his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his adoptive father, and the gods, each for something specific. So the fitting thanks is his own kind: name one specific thing he gave you. For many readers it's this: you can talk to yourself firmly and kindly, in plain words, and get up again.

693.title: Where it worked
693.hook: where did Stoic practice actually change a day?
693.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a journal and note specific moments when a principle changed what they did, as evidence of progress rather than knowledge.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Arethas, the bishop who kept a worn copy of Marcus's notebook. Your line was to himself, to us.

What would count as evidence? A runner can show a race time. A baker can show the bread. A year of Stoic reading has no scoreboard. Its evidence is quieter: a sharp remark someone didn't make, a night someone slept instead of rehearsing an argument, a loss met a little more steadily. Nobody hands out medals for those, and they're easy to forget by the weekend. So today is for looking, on purpose, one at a time. Where did it actually work?
screen: `NO SCOREBOARD FOR THIS.` → `A SHARP REMARK, NOT MADE.` → `WHERE DID IT ACTUALLY WORK?`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics' own test. Epictetus was blunt about where progress shows. Not in how many books you've read, he says in the Discourses, but in what you do with your desires and fears, in how you meet the day. In the Handbook he gives a picture: sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they ate. They digest it, and give wool and milk. So the question isn't what you know about Stoicism. It's where the wool showed. Second, the evidence is small. Look back down the year at the tools: a reply delayed, from Stoic in anger. A worry sorted into two columns, from Stoic at work. The evening questions, asked kindly. The view from above, for a night when something feels enormous. These are tiny hinges. A door swings on them anyway. Third, be specific. A vague sense that it helped won't hold up on a hard day. A real moment will: a time, a place, what you would have done, what you did instead. Marcus wrote book one that way: not my teachers were good, but from this one person, this one thing. Fourth, the week behind you: three habits to keep, one idea to leave, the first page reread, and thanks to a freed slave, a flawed courtier, and an emperor who wrote to himself. Today is for the proof, in your own life, that any of it mattered. Tomorrow, just as honestly, the other side.
screen: `THE TEST: WHERE THE WOOL SHOWED.` · `SMALL HINGES SWING BIG DOORS.` · `A TIME, A PLACE, A CHOICE.` · `A WEEK OF KEEPING AND THANKS.` · then, large: `IT WORKED HERE.`

segments.voice: Let the year scroll back slowly, looking not for a big transformation but for one moment: a reply you held back, a worry you set down, a morning that began with an intention instead of your phone. When one comes, stay with it: where were you, what would you have done before, and what did you do? If nothing comes, that's worth knowing too.
Discourses, Epictetus's teaching where progress shows not in books read but in a reply delayed, a worry sorted, a moment met well. Today's word.
Your line: it worked here. If someone asks what a year of this gave you, that moment is your answer. That's day six hundred ninety-three.
